title: Interrupts, Traps & Exceptions
summary: The three ways control reaches the kernel — interrupts, traps, and exceptions — and how the OS handles them without losing whatever the CPU was doing.

slides.markdown:
Control reaches the kernel exactly three ways: an **interrupt** from hardware (a key was pressed), a **trap** deliberately requested by software ([system calls](system-calls)), or an **exception** from something going wrong mid-instruction (division by zero). All three funnel into the same underlying mechanism — stop what you're doing, jump to a kernel handler, resume or terminate.

This topic covers the general mechanism that gets control into the kernel for all three; device-specific I/O handling once you're there lives in I/O & Device Management.

slides.sectionTitle: Interrupts vs traps vs exceptions — the three ways control reaches the kernel
slides.markdown:
All three stop normal execution and hand control to the kernel, but they differ in who triggers them and when.

| | Trigger | Timing | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interrupt | External hardware device | Asynchronous — any time, unrelated to current instruction | Keyboard press, network packet arrival, timer tick |
| Trap | Deliberate software instruction | Synchronous — the program requests it | A `syscall` instruction |
| Exception | An error during instruction execution | Synchronous — caused by the very instruction running | Divide by zero, invalid memory access |

**How to tell them apart in practice:** ask whether the CPU was told to stop (trap), was forced to stop by its own bad instruction (exception), or was interrupted by something entirely outside the currently running program (interrupt).

slides.sectionTitle: Hardware interrupts: how a device gets the CPU's attention
slides.markdown:
A device — a keyboard, a network card, a disk controller — has no way to "call a function" in the CPU. Instead, it asserts a signal on a physical **interrupt line** wired to the CPU (or, on modern systems, routed through an interrupt controller like the APIC). The CPU checks this line between instructions and, if it's asserted, pauses whatever it's running.

Critically, this happens **asynchronously** — a network packet can arrive while the CPU is in the middle of totally unrelated work for a totally unrelated process, and the interrupt doesn't wait for a convenient moment.

This is the mechanism that makes I/O efficient: a CPU can issue a disk read and go do other work entirely, trusting the disk to interrupt it later rather than sitting in a loop checking (see the polling-vs-interrupts slide).

slides.sectionTitle: Interrupt Service Routines (ISR) and the interrupt vector table
slides.markdown:
Just like syscalls use a syscall table, interrupts use an **interrupt vector table** (on x86, the IDT — Interrupt Descriptor Table): an array indexed by interrupt number, where each entry points to a specific **Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)** — the kernel code that handles that particular interrupt.

When an interrupt fires, the CPU hardware automatically saves the current instruction pointer and flags, looks up the ISR address in the vector table using the interrupt's number, and jumps there — all without any software having to search for the right handler.

This table-driven design is why adding support for a new device mostly means registering a new ISR at boot, not rewriting how interrupts are dispatched in general.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: interrupt handling timeline — device signal to CPU to ISR to resume
slides.markdown:
![Interrupt handling timeline with latency](assets/interrupt-timeline.svg)

The critical property this timeline shows: the interrupted process (A) has no idea an interrupt happened — its registers and program counter are restored exactly as they were, so from its perspective execution simply continued.

The gap between "device asserts interrupt" and "ISR starts running" is called **interrupt latency**, and it's a number real-time system designers measure and bound carefully (see Real-Time Scheduling).

Most interrupts are **maskable** — the CPU can be told (via a flag, `cli`/`sti` on x86) to temporarily ignore them, which the kernel does briefly during critical sections where an interrupt arriving mid-update would corrupt a data structure.

A small set are **non-maskable (NMI)** — they cannot be disabled by software at all, reserved for conditions so severe that ignoring them would be worse than the disruption of handling them: hardware memory errors (ECC failures), watchdog timers detecting a hung system, or a "hard reset" request.

The design intent: maskable interrupts give the kernel brief, controlled windows of atomicity; NMIs exist specifically so nothing — not even a kernel deep in a critical section — can suppress a genuinely catastrophic hardware signal.

Not all interrupts are equally urgent, so hardware assigns **priority levels** — a timer tick might be lower priority than a hardware failure signal. When a higher-priority interrupt arrives while a lower-priority ISR is running, most architectures allow it to **nest**: the CPU pauses the current ISR (much like it paused the original process) and handles the more urgent one first.

Lower-priority interrupts arriving during a higher-priority ISR are typically held pending until that ISR finishes, rather than nesting — this prevents priority inversion at the interrupt level, where a less-urgent handler could delay a more-urgent one.

Designers tune ISRs to run as briefly as possible precisely because nesting depth and pending-interrupt queues aren't unlimited — a slow, high-priority ISR can delay everything below it in priority, however "paused" they technically are.

slides.sectionTitle: Polling vs interrupts — why interrupts usually win
slides.markdown:
**Polling** means the CPU repeatedly checks a device's status register in a loop — "is the disk done yet? is it done yet?" — burning CPU cycles the entire time it's waiting, even when the device won't be ready for milliseconds. **Interrupts** let the CPU do other work and be notified only when the device actually has something ready.

| | Polling | Interrupts |
|---|---|---|
| CPU cost while waiting | Wastes cycles continuously checking | Near zero — CPU is free until notified |
| Latency for the event | Depends on poll frequency | Very low, near-immediate |
| Best for | Extremely frequent, fast events (network cards under heavy load) | Infrequent or slow events (keyboard, disk) |

**How to decide:** for very high-frequency events, polling can actually win — this is exactly why Linux's `NAPI` network driver framework switches from interrupts to polling under heavy packet load, avoiding "interrupt storms" that would otherwise starve the CPU with handler overhead alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: doing too much work inside an ISR — top half vs bottom half
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "An ISR should just fully handle the event before returning — do all the work right there."

**Why it's wrong:** ISRs run with interrupts often disabled or at elevated priority, so a long-running ISR delays every other interrupt of equal or lower priority, and blocks the scheduler from running — a slow network-packet ISR can measurably increase latency for completely unrelated processes.

**Correct model:** split the work. Linux calls this **top half / bottom half**: the top half (the actual ISR) does the absolute minimum — acknowledge the device, copy the essential data, schedule follow-up work — then returns immediately, re-enabling interrupts. The **bottom half** (a `tasklet`, `softirq`, or workqueue) does the heavier processing later, at a point where interrupts are enabled and other work isn't blocked. A network card's ISR grabs the packet off the hardware and defers protocol processing to a softirq for exactly this reason.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: exceptions can be recoverable and re-executed
slides.markdown:
Not every exception kills a process. A **page fault** — accessing a virtual address with no physical page currently mapped — is technically an exception (the CPU couldn't complete the instruction as issued), but it's a completely routine, recoverable one: the kernel's fault handler brings the needed page into memory (from disk, or by zeroing a fresh page), fixes up the page table, and then **re-executes the exact same instruction**, which now succeeds transparently.

This is the mechanism underneath demand paging, copy-on-write, and memory-mapped files — from the process's perspective, it just reads a memory address; underneath, it may have silently triggered disk I/O via a page fault exception. Contrast this with a divide-by-zero exception, which the kernel can't fix up (there's no valid instruction to retry) and typically delivers as a fatal signal instead.

The distinction a staff engineer draws: "exception" doesn't mean "error" — it means "the CPU couldn't finish this instruction without kernel help," and whether that's recoverable depends entirely on which exception it is.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
Interrupt load is directly observable: `/proc/interrupts` on Linux shows a live count of every interrupt by device and CPU core, and a spike there — especially concentrated on one core — is a classic sign of a misbehaving driver or a network card overwhelming a single core's IRQ handling. Tuning `irqbalance` or manually pinning a high-traffic NIC's interrupts across multiple cores is a real production fix for exactly this.

Cloud database engines and high-performance networking stacks (DPDK) go further and disable interrupts for their hot path entirely, polling dedicated cores instead — trading CPU cycles for eliminating interrupt latency and jitter altogether, the mirror image of the polling-vs-interrupts trade-off from earlier in this topic, chosen deliberately because packet rates are high enough that polling wins.

When a service shows oddly high, unexplained kernel-mode CPU time under network load, checking `/proc/interrupts` for a lopsided distribution is often the fastest way to confirm it's interrupt handling, not application logic.
